slide_text: Sorting — Inventing Order Sorting looks like a solved problem: call and move on. But almost every important idea in algorithm design — nested loops, invariants, divide and conquer, trading memory for speed — shows up first in sorting. In this chapter you will invent five different sorting algorithms, measure them against each other, and discover why some are dramatically faster, and when you can beat all of them. Quick Check — Bubble Sort Complexity If bubble sort takes about 50 seconds to sort 10,000 numbers, roughly how long would it take to sort 100,000 numbers (10x more)? A. About 500 seconds (10x longer) B. About 5,000 seconds (100x longer) C. About 50,000 seconds (1000x longer) D. About the same — 50 seconds

fragments.text: Answer: B. Bubble sort is O(n²). When n grows 10x, the time grows 10² = 100x. So 50 × 100 = 5,000 seconds — over an hour.

The Best Case Run your on a list that is already sorted , counting comparisons (write , like you did for bubble sort). Already sorted list of length 1000: how many comparisons? Reversed list of length 1000: how many comparisons? Insertion sort is O(n²) in the worst case, but O(n) when the data is nearly sorted — which is why real-world sorts (like Python's Timsort) use it as a building block. Hint When the list is already sorted, each new card is already in the right place, so the inner while loop does zero swaps — just one comparison per card, giving roughly n comparisons total.

Quick Check — Stability in Sorting Two students both scored 85: Alice (entered first) and Bob (entered second). After sorting by score, a stable sort guarantees Alice still appears before Bob. Which of the following is true? A. Bubble sort and insertion sort are stable, but quicksort is not (in its typical implementation) B. All comparison sorts are stable by definition C. Stability only matters for numbers, not for records with multiple fields D. Quicksort is stable but bubble sort is not

fragments.text: Answer: A. Bubble sort and insertion sort only swap adjacent elements and never swap equal elements past each other, so they preserve the original order of ties. Quicksort's partitioning can move equal elements across each other, making it unstable.

Quick Check — Quicksort Worst Case Quicksort is O(n·log n) on average, but what input causes its worst-case O(n²) performance when always picking the first element as pivot? A. A list of random numbers B. A list that is already sorted (or reverse-sorted) C. A list with many duplicate values D. A very short list (fewer than 5 elements)

fragments.text: Answer: B. When the list is already sorted and you always pick the first element as pivot, every partition puts 0 elements on one side and n-1 on the other. You get n levels of recursion instead of log(n), making it O(n²).

slide_text: Part 5: Sorting Without Comparing A puzzle: You must sort the ages of a billion people . Ages are whole numbers between 0 and 200. Write that returns the sorted list using — no comparisons between elements at all. [code block] Then answer: How many operations for n ages with values up to k? Quick Check — When O(n) Sorting Is Possible Counting sort can sort a billion ages in O(n) time. Why can't we always use it instead of O(n·log n) algorithms like merge sort? A. Counting sort only works on Python lists, not NumPy arrays B. Counting sort requires knowing the range of values and works best when that range is small — sorting a billion arbitrary floating-point numbers would need impossibly many buckets C. Counting sort is unstable, so we can't use it for important data D. Counting sort uses too much memory for any list larger than 1,000 elements

fragments.text: Answer: B. Counting sort needs an array of size k (the range of values). For ages 0-200, that is just 201 slots. But for arbitrary floats, the "range" is effectively infinite — you cannot create a counts array large enough. That is why comparison-based O(n·log n) sorts remain essential.

Part 7: Summary

What You Just Invented You built Real name Time Key idea you discovered Bubble sort O(n²) swap out-of-order neighbors, repeat; largest bubbles to end each pass Insertion sort O(n²), O(n) if nearly sorted insert each card into a sorted hand; building block of Timsort Merge sort O(n·log n) sort halves recursively, merge; needs extra memory Quick sort O(n·log n) average partition around a pivot, recurse; in place Counting sort O(n + k) count values, rebuild; no comparisons — only for small integer ranges
Python's built-in (Timsort) combines two of your inventions: merge sort's structure with insertion sort's speed on nearly-sorted runs.
Part 8: Reflection — What Did You Just Build?

Reflection Take a moment to answer these questions in your own words. You invented five sorting algorithms. In one sentence each, what is the core idea behind bubble sort, insertion sort, and merge sort? Why is O(n·log n) so much faster than O(n²) for large lists? What makes the divide-and-conquer approach (merge sort, quick sort) achieve this speedup? Insertion sort is O(n²) in the worst case but O(n) when data is nearly sorted. Why does this matter in practice? Counting sort bypasses the O(n·log n) barrier by not comparing elements at all. What assumption does it need, and when does that assumption break down? If you had to sort a million names alphabetically, which of your five algorithms would you pick, and why?
